item.description:

They weren't the only ones as the financing problems are underscoring how difficult it will be to find all the capital for the promised AI build out. The SOX chip index fell for an eighth day.

The oil market was more of a mystery as prices jumped higher in the US afternoon. The usual culprits are being pointed at, with the risks of a US escalation in Iran on the weekend. Even with that, the bond market was taking more of its cues from equities as yields ended the day lower. Earlier, Warsh didn't offer much in how he was leaning ahead of the upcoming meeting but that was generally seen as an endorsement of current market pricing.

In FX, the US dollar slumped again in another sign of the correlation between AI investment and the dollar. It's remarkable to see NZD as the top performer on a day while US major indexes were down 1-2% and it highlights the upending of the old paradigm. 

The weekly decline in the Nasdaq 100 was the largest since April 2025.

The week ahead features a pickup in earnings releases, including Meta and Tesla. Have a great weekend.

item.title: Oil prices surge higher into the weekend
item.description:
It will be another weekend of pain at the fuel pumps.

WTI crude oil is finishing the week at the highest since September 21 and back over $100 per barrel. WTI last trade up $3.33 to $101.30. Brent crude also touched $110 for the first time since May.

The strong rally to $101 from $98 in the final hours of trading today suggsets lingering worries about US attacks on Iran, particularly after all the news floated this week about the US military preparing MOAB attacks. Trump himself didn't push back against the reports when given the opportunity but he also previously wrote that the US won't attack Iran before the midterms. 

At the same time, things aren't looking great for Republicans in the polls and today the White House announced that new press secretary Katie Zacharia was asked to step down after just five days. We also learned today the US 2026 fiscal year deficit was the highest in five years. Trump may see fresh attacks as a Hail Mary opportunity to try to change the narrative around the war and inflation. 

Alternatively, Iran could try to escalate in order to further drive up oil prices and exact a toll on global consumers in order to gain leverage. 

In any case, there is no real catalyst in the news for today's big gain in oil. What it's doing is reverberating back into stock and bond markets and driving one of the worst days of the year in the Nasdaq, which was last down 2.2%.

Technically, WTI faces resistance at the September high of $106.75 with some breathing room before then. The war high was $119.48 in early March, though the high close was $112.95 as some of the days during the war were extremely volatile.

If nothing happens in the next couple weeks in oil, the focus will turn towards the post-midterms landscape. The vote is November 3 and the results of the vote could determine what happens next, with some reports saying Trump could make Secretary of Defense Pete Hegseth a scapegoat. What worries is that the vote doesn't change the equation much unless remaining Republicans insist that Trump ends it.

This article was written by Adam Button at investinglive.com.

item.title: US fiscal 2026 budget deficit was the largest in five years
item.description:
• September 2025 was a $198B surplus
  • Outlays $585B vs $346B a year ago
  • Receipts $558B vs $544B a year ago
  • FY2026 deficit $1.992 trillion vs $1.775T in FY2025, the largest in five years
  • FY2026 gross interest on the debt: record $1.36T, up $144B (12%)

Interest is now the main driver of the deficit. The $144B rise in interest costs accounts for about two-thirds of the $217B increase in the full-year shortfall. Treasury will keep rolling debt at higher rates while the Fed is debating hikes rather than cuts, so that line has nowhere to go but up.

The customs numbers are the most interesting part of the release. Gross customs receipts were $25.27B, roughly in line with the recent run rate. But refunds of $19.36B ate up 77% of that, leaving net customs receipts of just $5.91B.

The monthly swing from a $198B surplus to a $27B deficit is mostly about outlays, which jumped $239B y/y while receipts rose only 2.6%. Year-ago September comparisons are notoriously noisy because of payment timing, so the full-year number is the one that matters.

In any case, the headline tells most of the story as the US is in a huge fiscal hole and these are the good times for growth right now. There are going to be some very ugly days ahead and there's no way to grow out of it.

This article was written by Adam Button at investinglive.com.

item.title: The broader US stock indices are lower but showing different degrees of technical bias
item.description:
The major US stock indices are moving lower today as inflation concerns continue to weigh on sentiment. Technology shares are leading the declines:

  • Nasdaq Composite: down 1.15%.

  • Nasdaq 100: down 1.30%.

  • S&P 500: down 0.42%.

But the declines do not tell the whole story. From a technical perspective, each index has a different roadmap. Where is the risk? What would give buyers more control? What would open the door for further selling?

S&P 500: Waiting for the next shove

  • The S&P remains between its 100-hour moving average at 7746.68 and its 200-hour moving average at 7706.33.

  • Between those levels, the shorter-term bias is neutral. Buyers and sellers are battling it out, waiting for the next shove.

  • A move above—and sustained trading above—7746.68 would tilt the bias more to the upside. A break below 7706.33 would give sellers more control.

Nasdaq Composite: Sellers have the advantage, but daily support remains

  • The Nasdaq Composite is comfortably below its 200-hour moving average at 26827.18 and its 100-hour moving average at 27116.00. That keeps the shorter-term technical advantage with sellers.

  • Buyers need to reclaim those levels, starting with the lower 200-hour moving average, to begin improving the technical picture.

  • However, the index remains above its rising 100-day moving average at 26288.75. That is a key downside risk level. Hold above it, and buyers retain a foothold. Break below and stay below, and the door opens for further selling momentum.

Nasdaq 100: Sellers remain firmly in control

  • The Nasdaq 100 has moved away from its hourly moving averages and is also breaking below its 100-day moving average at 29624.02.

  • Today’s low of 29452.10 has already taken out yesterday’s low—and the previous weekly low—at 29554. Sellers have extended the downside. The question now is whether they can sustain that break.

  • Staying below 29554 keeps pressure on the index. Moving back above that level would ease some immediate pressure, but buyers would still need to reclaim the 100-day moving average at 29624.02 to begin repairing the technical damage.

The lesson: Let the levels define the bias

A lower market does not automatically mean every index has the same bearish bias. The S&P is still between its hourly moving averages. The Nasdaq Composite is below those averages but holding above daily support. The Nasdaq 100 is breaking below that daily support as well.

Those differences matter. The technical levels help traders define risk, judge who has control, and identify what needs to change.

In the video above, I take a closer look at the key technical levels, the risks, and the targets, and outline the roadmap for traders.

This article was written by Greg Michalowski at investinglive.com.

item.title: Flying car. Grounded stock. The technicals are not leaning to a "take-off" for Tesla stock
item.description:
The flying car gets attention. But is it good for business?

Tesla’s flying car has certainly brought out the “oohs” and “aahs.” And why not? A car that can briefly take flight is going to get attention. From a marketing perspective, that is a win for Tesla. It gets people talking and gives Elon Musk another opportunity to show what his engineers can do.

But is it good for the business?

That is where I have some questions. How many people need a flying sports car? How much will it cost to develop and produce? Could that money—and engineering talent—be better spent on vehicles that more people can afford and use every day? Will the flying version ever get approved for public use? Or is it simply a gimmick?

I am still waiting for the flux capacitor and the time-machine capability.

Nevertheless, the publicity has value. The payoff for shareholders is less clear.

Elon had his moment. Now the market gets its turn.

Which brings me to the technicals.

Despite all the excitement, the price action helps tell us whether the market is buying the idea—or selling it. And Tesla’s technical picture is not overly bullish.

The car got off the ground. Can the stock do the same?

Let’s look at the levels.

Elon Musk had his moment yesterday. Today, the market gets its turn.

At the open, Tesla shares moved higher, reaching $370.58. However, that high fell just short of the 100-day moving average at $371.13. Buyers had their shot to test that key technical target. They could not get above it.

The price has since rotated lower, reaching $360.20. It is currently trading near $361.50, down about $1 on the day.

Moving averages give sellers something to lean against

In the process, the price also moved back below the near-converged 100- and 200-hour moving averages at $368.85. That gives traders a clear level to watch on any rebound.

Stay below those hourly moving averages, and the sellers retain control. Get above them, and the buyers get another opportunity to challenge the 100-day moving average at $371.13. Getting above—and staying above—that level would strengthen the bullish case.

So far, however, the 100-day moving average has capped the rally, and the hourly moving averages have given way. That does not speak to buyers taking control. It gives the sellers more confidence.

Opinions are one thing. The price action defines the risk.

Now, my questions about the flying car’s viability are simply my thoughts. Others will be more bullish on the idea and excited about a car that can take flight or accelerate from 0 to 60 mph in less than a second.

I still ask: Where exactly are you going to use that? Preferably somewhere without big, fat trees along the side of the road or any cars in sight.

As traders and investors, however, we need to bring the focus back to price. The chart gives us a roadmap. The technical tools help define the risk, the bias and the next targets.

Right now, that roadmap shows Tesla:

  • Below its 100- and 200-hour moving averages near $368.85.

  • Below its 100-day moving average at $371.13.

  • Below its 200-day moving average near $388.02.

What would get the stock off the ground?

There is work to do.

If the stock is going to get off the ground technically, the buyers need to reclaim those moving averages, starting with the hourly levels, and stay above them. Then the 100 day MA and ultimately the 200 day MA at $388.  

Until then, the stock remains grounded, and the sellers remain more in control.

This article was written by Greg Michalowski at investinglive.com.

item.title: Earnings week ahead: Banks were upbeat on the economy, now onto tech
item.description:
The big banks set the tone this week: consumers are still spending, businesses are borrowing again, and credit isn’t getting worse. That’s good for growth, but it isn’t the demand destruction the Fed may need. September CPI came in at 3.7% headline and 2.6% core, both above forecast, and futures now price October no-change at 73%. The FOMC meets October 27–28, so next week’s earnings are the last real-economy check before the decision.

Monday, Oct 19

Before market:Cleveland-Cliffs shows auto-sector steel demand and whether tariff protection still translates into pricing. Steel prices are up 52% year-over-year so there is a nice tailwind there but their Canadian operations are struggling due to tariffs. Fifth Third opens the second wave of regionals.

After market:Zions, Western Alliance, Wintrust and BOK Financial close out bank week. The big banks were clean, so watch deposit costs after the September hike and commercial real estate charge-offs. Steel Dynamics quietly signals nonresidential construction and should be a better view than CLF on overall demand.

Tuesday, Oct 20

Before market:GM is the big one. Auto prices helped push up core CPI. Is that pricing power or tariff pass-through, and how much are higher financing costs hurting buyers? 3M is the short-cycle industrial bellwether and a company that's been struggling for a decade. Halliburton shows whether higher oil is pulling North American drilling back or whether capital discipline holds, which matters for how long the energy shock lasts. GE Aerospace, RTX and Northrop cover defence and the aerospace aftermarket.

After market:Netflix tests pricing power but note that on Friday they fired their chief content officer in a move that highlights some audience problems. Capital One is another consumer credit read. United and Alaska Airlines are good crosschecks on the strong demand that Delta talked about. Premium versus main-cabin commentary will show who is still spending but jet fuel is a major drag.

Wednesday, Oct 21

Before market:NextEra carries the power-demand story: data center load growth against rate-sensitive financing. It could be telling for the whole AI trade. CME gains from rate-futures volatility. Moody’s reads corporate issuance after the bond wobble.

After market:Tesla and Meta are the first big tech names to report and that should be a good check on market sentiment. The broader signal on the economy and AI is Texas Instruments. Its guidance is the best broad read on the industrial and auto chip cycle. A soft Q4 outlook would spell problems. Lam also covers semi capex and China. CSX covers freight volumes on the rails and will be one I'm watching. Southwest and Wyndham show the middle- and lower-income traveller, who could be pulling back.

Thursday, Oct 22

Before market:Procter & Gamble is the key staples report of the quarter, and volume versus price is the whole story. Flat volumes on higher prices would mean the consumer is being squeezed. Union Pacific and Norfolk Southern report the same morning, with freight volumes and the pending merger in focus. Blackstone covers private credit and real estate as rates rise; if tightening breaks something, look there. Honeywell, Lockheed and Comcast round it out.

After market:Robert Half is the sleeper macro report of the week, because temp staffing turns before payrolls do. Weak commentary would undercut the “healthy consumer because healthy jobs” argument. Bloom Energy and Western Digital are the AI infrastructure trade and will lead to some big swings in those stocks.

Friday, Oct 23

Before market:American Express shows the affluent consumer, who has carried spending all year. Slowing billings would be a problem at the top of the K. For Canada, Rogers shows subscriber growth now that population growth has slowed sharply. Telcos have been struggling badly but the company could monetize its sports team ownership.

This article was written by Adam Button at investinglive.com.

item.title: Bitcoin is little changed on the day, and pushing against a key crossroad. What next?
item.description:
Bitcoin has spent the early part of the week moving back and forth across its 100- and 200-hour moving averages (they are near converged near $82,500). Each modest break above offered an opportunity for the buyers to take control. However, sellers prevailed.  The price moved away from those moving averages and lower, but similarly to the buyers at the high resistance, sellers reached support and found momentum faded as well. And true to form, the price pushed higher. 

Now the price is back at those converged moving averages near $82,500, putting traders at the same key crossroad at the 100 and 200 hour moving averages.

A week of missed opportunities

Bitcoin started the week above its 100-hour moving average and testing its higher 200-hour moving average—the green line on the chart below. Monday’s push briefly cleared that level, but the rally stalled at $84,178. Buyers could not keep the momentum going, and the price reversed below the 100-hour moving average toward swing support between $80,106 and $81,183.

After finding support in that area on Tuesday, buyers took another run to the upside. The rebound carried the price back above both moving averages, shifting the short-term bias in their favor. However, the rally failed to take out Monday’s high at $84,178.

The buyers had their shot. They could not finish the job.

That failure kept sellers in play and they pushed lower. On Wednesday, the price broke below the then-converged moving averages near $83,100, and downside momentum accelerated. By Thursday, bitcoin had fallen through the bottom of the $80,106–$81,183 swing area.

That should have opened the door for further selling. Instead, the break quickly ran out of steam, and the price snapped back above the support zone.

This time, the sellers had their shot. They missed.

Back at the moving-average crossroads

The recovery has now brought bitcoin back to its converged 100- and 200-hour moving averages near $82,500. Those levels are being tested today, and the next move needs follow-through.

For buyers, the job is to get above those moving averages—and stay above them. A sustained break would shift the short-term bias higher and put the following targets in play:

  • $84,178: Monday’s high and the ceiling buyers failed to clear earlier this week.

  • $85,578–$87,374: The higher resistance area containing the September and October cycle highs.

For sellers, the job is to keep a lid on the price at the moving averages. If they can do that and push the price lower, the focus returns to:

  • $81,183–$80,106: The swing support area that has been central to this week’s trading.

  • $76,052: The 38.2% retracement of the rally from the July low to the September high, if support gives way and sellers sustain the break.

The trading lesson: A break needs staying power

This week is a reminder that trading through a technical level is only the first step. What happens after the break matters.

Buyers moved above the moving averages but failed to clear the weekly high. Sellers broke below swing support but could not keep the price down. Both failures led to reversals.

Now bitcoin is back at the crossing. Get and stay above $82,500, and buyers have another opportunity to take control. Stay below, and sellers retain the advantage at resistance.

The levels define the risk. The follow-through will tell us who is taking control.

This article was written by Greg Michalowski at investinglive.com.

item.title: US September industrial production +0.7% vs +0.4% expected
item.description:
• Prior was 0.0% (revised to +0.1%)
  • Capacity utilization 76.9% vs 76.5% exp
  • Manufacturing output +0.3% vs +0.3% exp
  • Prior manufacturing output -0.3% (revised to -0.2%)
  • Mining +0.2%
  • Utilities +3.5%
  • Machinery +1.4%, primary metals +1.6%, electrical equipment +1.3%, chemicals +1.0%.

The headline is flattered by utilities. Electric utility output jumped 3.7% m/m and is up 9.6% y/y, and the utility operating rate rose 2.3 points to 73.8%. That could be weather, but the year-over-year trend is consistent with data center load. Utilities output rose at a 14.8% annualized pace in Q3.

Manufacturing is a two-speed story:

  • Semiconductor output rose 2.1% m/m and is up 19.9% y/y. It grew at a 28.4% annualized rate in Q3, which drove most of the 3.8% gain in durables.
  • Excluding high-tech, factory output rose just 0.2% m/m and is up only 0.7% y/y.
  • Motor vehicles and parts fell 3.0%, with vehicles down 5.4%. Assemblies fell to a 10.21m annual rate from 10.61m in August and 11.0m in May. Excluding autos, manufacturing rose 0.5%.

AI is truly eating the world and it's masking the undercurrents in the rest of the economy. Unfortunately, monetary policy is a blunt instrument and hiking rates to cool off inflation is going to hit the rest of the economy hard, including the struggling motor vehicle and overall manufacturing economy ex-tech. The better way to handle this would be on the fiscal side with some austerity but that's not coming.

This article was written by Adam Button at investinglive.com.

item.title: USDCAD is lower on the day, but getting a modest lift after another higher inflation reading
item.description:
The USDCAD has seen plenty of up-and-down price action this week, but one message has been consistent: buyers have struggled to sustain momentum near the highs for the year.

The highs from October 5 and October 9 established a ceiling near 1.4292–1.4298. Monday’s high fell short at 1.4286. On Wednesday, the stronger-than-expected CPI data gave buyers another opportunity to push higher, but the rally stalled at 1.4298.

From there, the price rotated lower and closed back below the 100- and 200-hour moving averages near 1.4244.

Go figure. Stronger inflation. A lower USDCAD.

Yesterday’s higher-than-expected PPI data did not turn the tide either. Instead, the pair extended its decline, breaking below a key floor between 1.41922 and 1.4204.

Technical levels do matter. The buyers could not get through the ceiling. Once the moving averages and floor gave way, sellers had more control.

A longer-term support area gives buyers a place to lean

The selling continued today, taking the price into a swing area between 1.41297 and 1.4153.

That area supported the pair from mid-June into mid-July and also lines up with swing highs from November 2025. Today’s low reached 1.4146, putting the price inside that support zone.

The import/export price data provided another sign of inflation pressure—and another opportunity for traders to buy the US dollar.

Take a look at these concerns.

  • Fuel and lubricants: +34.5%. Natural gas rose 96.5%, although its small weight—roughly 0.3%—limits its overall influence.
  • Industrial supplies and materials: +20.4%.
  • Unfinished metals: +25.3%; finished metals: +18.5%.
  • Industrial supplies excluding fuels: +13.0%.
  • Nonelectrical machinery: +10.4%; capital goods: +8.4%.
  • Imports excluding food and fuels: +6.2%.

Food, autos and consumer goods are comparatively less troublesome: annual increases were 2.9%, 1.1% and 2.7%, respectively.

Import takeaway: The persistent concern is the cost of equipment and production inputs. Energy explains September’s biggest jump, but it does not explain away the broader inflation pressure.

The USD is finding a bid.  The difference this time?

Although the USD moved lower on the CPI and the PPI, today we are seeing a modest bid.  Why?  The USDCAD had already moved lower from its highs for the year and reached an established technical support area. Buyers now have a level against which to define their risk.

The question is whether they "can hold the support?".

A move back above 1.4153, followed by an ability to stay above it, would strengthen the case for a bounce. While the price remains inside the zone, buyers and sellers are still battling.

The lower boundary at 1.41297 is the key downside risk level. Stay above it, and buyers retain an opportunity to build a recovery. Move below it and stay below, and another layer of support gives way, opening the door for further selling.

What would a recovery need to clear?

On further upside momentum, the targets come in at:

  • 1.41922–1.4204: The broken floor. Prior support becomes potential resistance.

  • 1.4223: The falling 100-hour moving average.

  • 1.4233: The falling 200-hour moving average.

Holding support is a start. Getting back above those resistance levels would provide evidence that buyers are taking back control.

The trading lesson: Prepare before you trade

Hotter inflation data can give traders a reason to buy the dollar. It does not guarantee that the price will move higher—or stay higher.

item.title: US September import price index +1.1% vs +0.8% expected
item.description:
• Prior was +0.7% m/m (revised to +0.5%)
  • Export prices +2.2% vs +1.0% expected
  • Prior export prices were +0.6% (revised to +1.2%)
  • Import prices y/y 8.1%  vs +7.0% prior

It's been an ugly week for inflation data. The market seems to think the Fed can tame it by waiting until December but that's some serious imported inflation that's going to be working its way through prices for awhile.

The Bureau of Labor Statistics publishes the import and export price indexes  monthly. They measure what US buyers pay for foreign goods and services and what foreign buyers pay for American output. The data rarely moves markets on its own, but it is a useful read on how the dollar, global commodity prices and foreign producer costs are feeding into the US economy. One point worth knowing: import prices exclude tariffs and duties. That makes the series a clean test of whether foreign exporters are absorbing tariff costs or passing them through. It is also one of the inputs used to deflate trade in the GDP accounts.

In August, import prices rose 0.7%, and energy dominated. Import fuel prices were up 26.8% from a year earlier, and natural gas import prices more than doubled, rising 102.6%. Export prices climbed 8.6% over the 12 months to August. China stands out: import prices from China rose 1.0% in August, the biggest monthly gain since the series started in January 2004.

The September report follows two hot inflation prints this week. Headline CPI rose to 3.7% y/y against 3.6% expected, with core at 2.6% versus a 2.5% forecast and a 0.33% monthly gain. Energy jumped 5.2% on the month, and a 9.1% surge in gasoline accounted for more than half the overall increase. PPI was worse. Producer prices rose 1.3% m/m and 6.3% y/y, far above the consensus of 0.5% and 5.3%. That was the fastest monthly increase since March 2022 and the highest annual rate since December 2022.

This article was written by Adam Button at investinglive.com.

item.title: BOJ’s Ueda: We will continue to raise rates as underlying inflation approaches 2%
item.description:
• Want to gauge neutral rate estimate taking into account accumulative impact of past rate hikes on financial conditions, domestic prices
  • Hard to say anything clear about Japan’s neutral rate of interest
  • Takeaway from this week’s meetings was to exchange views with other policymakers on how Middle East conflict and AI demand could affect global, Japanese economies and inflation
  • As we have said, our policy has entered a new phase as underlying inflation is quite close to 2%, we cannot allow inflation to rise further
  • As underlying inflation is quite close to 2%, it is becoming more important than before to anchor inflation around our target
  • Haven’t been in touch with US Treasury Secretary Bessent since we met in Asheville
  • Timing, pace of future rate hikes will be decided looking at impact of FX, AI demand and Middle East developments on prices
  • We will discuss at upcoming meeting whether to tweak our assessment that underlying inflation is approaching 2%
  • Did not hear anything at this week’s meetings that deviated from our baseline view
  • Economic, price moves roughly in line with our forecasts
  • We will continue to raise interest rates as underlying inflation approaching 2%, financial conditions are accommodative
  • I felt that there were more policymakers at this meeting who were somewhat more bullish on AI demand than we had estimated
  • No big gap in view between what we have assessed on inflationary pressure from AI demand, and what I heard from global policymakers

Bank of Japan Governor Kazuo Ueda said at the IMF meetings that the BOJ will continue to raise interest rates, with underlying inflation approaching 2% and financial conditions still accommodative. The BOJ policy rate is currently at 1.25% and the market sees little chance of a hike at the October 30 meeting but that rises to 75% for the December 18 meeting.

Ueda said policy has entered a new phase and that the BOJ cannot allow inflation to rise further. With underlying inflation quite close to target, anchoring it around 2% is becoming more important than before. He said the BOJ will discuss at its upcoming meeting whether to tweak its assessment that underlying inflation is approaching 2%.

The timing and pace of future hikes will depend on the impact of FX, AI demand and Middle East developments on prices. Economic and price moves are roughly in line with BOJ forecasts, and he said nothing he heard at this week’s meetings deviated from the baseline view.

On AI, Ueda said more policymakers than expected were bullish on AI demand, but there was no big gap between the BOJ’s assessment of AI-driven inflation pressure and what he heard from global counterparts.

He said Japan’s neutral rate remains hard to pin down. Ueda exchanged views with Fed Chair Warsh but declined to comment on the discussion, and said he hasn’t been in touch with Treasury Secretary Bessent since they met in Asheville, which is notable on the intervention front.

USD/JPY is flat today at 158.00 while the US dollar is broadly weaker elsewhere.

This article was written by Adam Button at investinglive.com.

We've haven't seen major changes in interest rate expectations this week. The Bank of England and Reserve Bank of New Zealand saw a slightly hawkish repricing, while the Federal Reserve and the Reserve Bank of Australia moved in a more dovish direction. Expectations for the European Central Bank, Bank of Canada and Swiss National Bank remained unchanged.

The BoE saw a modest hawkish repricing as markets reinforced expectations of a rate hike in November after a good UK GDP report. Governor Bailey recently said that second-round effects from higher energy prices appeared subdued so far, but warned that it was still too early to draw firm conclusions. So, the central bank remains cautiously hawkish.

The RBNZ also saw a slightly hawkish repricing on concerns that higher energy costs could keep inflation elevated for longer and therefore require further monetary tightening. As a reminder, the RBNZ raised its policy rate to 2.75% in September citing inflation above target range and an economic recovery that appeared to be resuming. Although weaker household spending and labour market slack remain key risks, the RBNZ has indicated that further increases may be needed if inflation pressures persist.

On the Federal Reserve side, despite the higher than expected US inflation data, we saw a minor dovish repricing, especially further out the curve. Treasury yields fell following the inflation data, possibly suggesting that markets may be increasingly concerned about growth.

The RBA saw a dovish shift following Australia's September employment report. Employment unexpectedly fell by 39,300, while the unemployment rate remained at 4.7%, its highest level in five years. The report reduced expectations for another rate hike, with markets pricing a higher probability of the RBA holding rates steady for longer. The labour market conditions may be weakening enough to limit the need for further tightening, even as inflation remains a concern.

ECB rate expectations remained broadly unchanged, with no major new developments. The central bank continues to face the difficult balance between higher energy-driven inflation and the risk that prolonged supply disruptions will weaken economic activity. Moreover, the recent bond market woes strengthened the case for a more patient approach following the recent tightening.

The BoC also saw little change in rate expectations. Canadian inflation and labour market data continue to support a patient approach on interest rates, especially given the ongoing tariff issues with the US.  

SNB expectations also remained stable, reflecting Switzerland's subdued underlying inflation and the recent Swiss franc's strength due to safe-haven flows. Keep in mind that astronger franc can help contain imported inflation, partly offsetting the impact of higher global energy prices. This mechanism is particularly strong for Swiss inflation.

This article was written by Giuseppe Dellamotta at investinglive.com.

And that now puts the spotlight back on the 5.00% level, which had previously played the role in keeping yields from breaking out back in September.

As such, it would require a firm daily close below 5.00% to deliver a stronger signal that the recent upward momentum is starting to unravel.

After which, that could open up a move towards 4.70%, where the 100-day moving average (red line) is also sticking nearby at 4.73%. Further below, the 200-day moving average (blue line) around 4.50% could come into consideration.

But for now, it's baby steps first. I wouldn't be too quick to call an end to the broader uptrend just yet.

10-year yields are still comfortably holding above the key 5.00% threshold in the past few sessions. And any semblance of a rebound back towards 5.20% or even 5.30% again would put the recent rejection back to the test.

And from a fundamental standpoint, nothing much has really changed. Inflation pressures are still holding up and the same structural factors underpinning yields since last month are also still very much in place. Heavy Treasury issuance and concerns about the long-term trajectory of US debt are key reasons why investors are demanding more compensation to hold longer-dated government bonds.

But at least for the time being, all eyes are turning back to the 5.00% mark as the line in the sand. Hold above and we're still talking about the upward pressure in yields being sustained for the most part. But break below, and this could turn the sharp pullback this week into something more meaningful perhaps.

This article was written by Justin Low at investinglive.com.

item.title: Dow Jones futures analysis: Fed risks and key levels for October 16
item.description:
Dow Jones futures recover, but can bulls overcome 52,612 amid Fed and inflation uncertainty?

Dow Jones futures are showing a more constructive technical picture on Friday, October 16, but the economic backdrop remains complicated. Federal Reserve uncertainty, persistent inflation, concerns about AI financing and changing bond-market expectations could influence the next move. Meanwhile, E-mini Dow futures are approaching an important resistance test around 52,612, with higher potential targets if buyers can sustain the recovery. Let's first jump into my Dow Jones futures technical analysis video right with the European market open:

What news could affect the Dow Jones today?

Several developments over the past 24 hours deserve attention. They do not necessarily explain every movement in Dow futures, but they help establish the conditions under which the technical recovery is taking place.

1. Fed Chair Warsh sounds optimistic but offers little interest-rate guidance

Federal Reserve Chair Kevin Warsh struck a relatively optimistic tone about the resilience of the US economy during Friday's remarks at the IMF meetings in Bangkok.

However, he avoided signaling what the Fed might do at its upcoming October 27-28 meeting or its December meeting.

This matters because the Fed raised its policy rate in September, while recent inflation readings have increased uncertainty about whether further tightening will be required.

As Eamonn Sheridan explains in Warsh won't prejudge rest of 2026, names October and December as decision points, the absence of clear guidance leaves investors more dependent on incoming economic data.

What could this mean for the Dow?

A resilient economy would generally support corporate revenue and earnings. But if the Fed keeps interest rates elevated, borrowing costs could remain a burden for businesses and consumers.

For traders, the important question is not simply whether Warsh sounds optimistic. It is whether economic resilience can continue without requiring monetary policy that becomes increasingly restrictive.

2. Inflation is becoming a corporate earnings question

Thursday's US Producer Price Index report showed producer prices rising 1.3% in September, the largest monthly increase since March 2022. Annual producer inflation reached 6.3%.

Meanwhile, retail sales rose 0.8% in September, apparently signaling a healthy consumer.

However, there is an important qualification.

Much of the headline retail-sales increase reflected higher gasoline spending. The closely watched retail-sales control group, which excludes several volatile categories, increased just 0.1%.

Furthermore, retail-sales figures are not adjusted for inflation. Spending more money does not necessarily mean consumers are buying more goods.

For the Dow, this creates two related risks.

First, companies could face higher transportation, energy and production costs. Second, customers may become more selective about what they buy.

Home Depot, Walmart and other consumer-facing businesses could feel the consequences differently, depending on their customers, pricing power and product mix.

Justin Low explains the underlying business problem in today's investingLive educational article, Why higher inflation doesn't always mean bigger corporate profits.

The takeaway for investors: During earnings season, revenue growth alone may not tell the full story. Sales volumes and operating margins could become more revealing, particularly if companies are struggling to pass higher costs on to customers.

3. Falling Treasury yields are not necessarily good news for stocks

One of the more interesting developments this week has been the behavior of the US bond market.

Despite stronger-than-expected inflation figures, Treasury yields have declined from their earlier highs.

Ordinarily, investors might expect inflation surprises to push yields higher as markets anticipate tighter monetary policy.

But another interpretation deserves consideration.

What if bond investors are becoming increasingly concerned that high borrowing costs and persistent inflation could eventually damage economic growth?

In today's analysis of whether the bond market is becoming more concerned about growth than inflation, Justin Low explores precisely that possibility.

This distinction matters for Dow investors.

Lower bond yields can support stock valuations by reducing discount rates and financing costs. However, when yields decline because investors are seeking safety or anticipating weaker economic activity, the implications for corporate earnings may be less favorable.

The useful distinction is why yields are falling, rather than merely whether they are falling.

For example, Caterpillar could benefit from easing financing conditions while simultaneously facing weaker equipment demand if businesses reduce investment.

These opposing influences help explain why the same economic development can have different effects across Dow constituents.

4. AI infrastructure demand remains strong, but financing concerns persist

Another development worth following comes from Europe.

On October 16, Schneider Electric raised its 2026 organic revenue-growth forecast to 12%-14%, citing strong demand for data-center infrastructure. Reuters reported that the company experienced triple-digit growth in data-center demand during the quarter.

That is encouraging evidence that physical infrastructure investment remains strong.

At the same time, recent concern about debt-financed AI expansion is raising questions about whether every company participating in the investment boom will achieve sufficient profitability.

For Dow constituents such as Nvidia and Microsoft, the distinction is important.

AI infrastructure demand can remain strong even while investors become more cautious about the financing, profitability and valuations of certain companies.

These are not necessarily contradictory signals.

Investors could watch whether strong orders continue to translate into sustainable revenue and cash flow, and whether financing concerns remain concentrated in highly leveraged businesses or begin affecting larger investment programs.

5. Oil and Middle East developments remain another source of uncertainty

Oil is particularly relevant because energy costs have contributed heavily to the latest inflation readings.

President Trump said he would rule out certain military actions against Iran while leaving the possibility of other strikes open.

As investingLive reported in Trump draws two red lines on Iran but keeps Pickaxe Mountain strike in play, uncertainty surrounding the Strait of Hormuz remains relevant to oil supply.

For the Dow, an escalation that materially increases energy costs could affect manufacturers, consumer spending and interest-rate expectations.

Conversely, sustained easing in oil supply risks could relieve some of those pressures, even if the broader inflation problem remains unresolved.

Why the Dow can behave differently from the broader stock market

There is another point worth remembering when interpreting these developments.

Unlike the market-capitalization-weighted S&P 500, the Dow Jones Industrial Average is price-weighted.

This means a stock with a higher share price generally has a larger percentage influence on the Dow than a lower-priced stock, regardless of the relative size of their companies.

As a result, strength in selected higher-priced constituents can support the Dow even when weakness develops elsewhere in the market.

That does not make the recovery insignificant. It does mean that traders should distinguish the Dow's index performance from the underlying health of the broader equity market.

Watching how industrial, financial, consumer and technology constituents respond to the same news can offer useful confirmation or reveal important divergences.

Dow Jones futures technical analysis: Buyers have improved their position

In my accompanying technical-analysis video, I examine the CBOT E-mini Dow Jones futures (YM) on the four-hour chart.

The technical observations reflect the European morning of October 16, with futures around 52,527 at approximately 09:29 Berlin time.

These are futures prices, not prices for the cash Dow Jones Industrial Average. The latest completed four-hour candle ended at 08:00 Berlin time, while the following candle was still developing.

A breakout, a retracement and a developing bullish recovery

The four-hour structure has improved noticeably.

Following lows around 50,859 on October 1 and 50,909 on October 8, futures began developing a recovery within a rising channel.

The chart also shows a breakout from a smaller corrective structure resembling a bullish flag, followed by a pullback that came close to retesting the breakout area.

That sequence is important.

A breakout on its own can attract buying, but the subsequent pullback provides additional information about whether buyers are willing to defend their earlier progress.

The October 14 decline toward 51,600 failed to develop into another test of the early-October lows. Instead, buyers reasserted themselves and futures recovered toward 52,500 by Friday's European morning.

The latest price structure therefore looks more constructive than it did earlier in the month.

However, an improving recovery is not the same as a confirmed breakout through overhead resistance.

Volume improves the bullish case, but there is an important qualification

The recovery has not occurred on insignificant trading activity.

A strong October 15 four-hour recovery candle traded approximately 45,500 futures contracts, exceeding the volume of comparable four-hour periods on October 13 and 14.

Momentum also improved, with the MACD moving above its signal line on October 15.

These observations suggest that buyers have recently become more effective.

But there is an important contrast.

The October 13 advance toward 52,612 also attracted substantial trading activity before sellers reversed the move.

In other words, both the earlier rejection and the subsequent recovery occurred with meaningful participation.

High trading volume shows activity. It does not, by itself, establish which side will ultimately prevail.

That brings us to the most important technical question for today.

Dow Jones futures: Key levels to watch

52,612: The previous rejection high

On October 13, futures reached approximately 52,612 before reversing sharply.

That level now represents the first important test of the recovery.

Buyers would strengthen their case by establishing a completed four-hour breakout above the previous high, followed by sustained trading above it or a successful retest.

A temporary move above resistance that quickly reverses would provide substantially less confirmation.

There is also a useful volatility consideration.

From the 09:29 snapshot around 52,527, the distance to 52,612 is only about 85 points. Recent four-hour average true range, a measure of trading volatility, was approximately 218 points.

Consequently, a brief move through 52,612 could occur within an otherwise ordinary four-hour trading range.

That makes the reaction after the initial test particularly important.

52,700 and 52,950: Potential bullish objectives

If the recovery continues and buyers overcome the previous rejection area, the technical map identifies two possible upside objectives.

52,700: The first potential bullish objective beyond the October 13 high.

52,950: A higher objective that also aligns with a significant historical trading-activity reference.

These levels are not predictions or automatic buy signals.

For traders already holding a profitable long position, they can serve as areas where partial profit-taking or reassessment may be considered, depending on the individual trading plan.

The important condition is that buyers first demonstrate sufficient strength to overcome the nearby resistance.

52,300-52,450: The first area for buyers to defend

If futures pull back instead of breaking higher, the 52,300-52,450 region is an initial support area worth monitoring.

Holding this area would suggest that buyers are still defending much of the recent recovery.

A sustained decline through it would weaken the immediate bullish picture and raise the possibility of a deeper retracement.

52,263: A previous trading-value reference

The video also highlights an important level near 52,263, associated with the value area of an earlier consolidation.

A value area represents a price region where a substantial share of trading occurred during a selected period.

Why does this matter?

When price moves back into a previous area of heavy trading, it can indicate that the market is revisiting prices where buyers and sellers previously found relatively broad agreement.

This does not automatically mean a reversal is coming.

However, it would be less encouraging for bulls than continued acceptance at higher prices.

52,150: A deeper swing-trading reference

Another level highlighted in the video is the four-hour 20-period exponential moving average, near 52,150 at the time of the analysis.

An exponential moving average gives greater weight to recent prices and can help traders evaluate the direction of a developing trend.

For a swing-trading perspective, I discuss using two consecutive completed four-hour candles below this reference as a more meaningful warning that the recovery is weakening, rather than reacting immediately to one isolated move below it.

That is a confirmation approach, not a guarantee. It may filter out temporary weakness, but it can also identify a reversal later than an earlier warning would.

If that broader support structure deteriorates, the 52,000-52,100 region becomes another relevant area to reassess.

What would strengthen or weaken the bullish outlook?

Bullish continuation

A completed four-hour move above 52,612, followed by sustained trading above the previous rejection area, would provide stronger confirmation that buyers have overcome an important obstacle.

That would increase the relevance of the 52,700 and 52,950 upside objectives.

An inconclusive breakout

A short-lived move above 52,612 that quickly returns below the prior high would be less convincing.

This would suggest that sellers remain active near resistance and that the recovery may require further consolidation.

A weakening recovery

Failure to defend 52,300-52,450, followed by deterioration near 52,263 and 52,150, would progressively weaken the bullish technical interpretation.

A deeper decline toward 52,000-52,100 would raise further questions about whether the recent advance is sustainable.

These scenarios describe areas to evaluate, not instructions that a trade must be placed at any particular price.

What could change the outlook during Friday's US session?

The latest macroeconomic uncertainty makes today's US economic releases particularly relevant.

Three developments deserve attention:

  • 14:30 Berlin time (08:30 New York): US import and export prices. Additional evidence of whether international pricing pressures are feeding into domestic inflation.

  • 15:15 Berlin time (09:15 New York): US industrial production and capacity utilization. A useful check on manufacturing activity and demand for industrial capacity.

  • Travelers (TRV) third-quarter results: Scheduled before the US market opens, with its earnings conference call at 15:00 Berlin time (09:00 New York). The insurer's results could provide a separate, company-specific influence on the price-weighted Dow.

The combination of these releases, Fed uncertainty and the technical resistance test creates several possible paths for Friday's US session.

A constructive industrial-production report accompanied by moderating inflation pressures could support confidence in the economic outlook.

Conversely, renewed inflation pressure or evidence of weakening industrial demand could complicate the recovery.

An especially informative outcome would be how Dow futures respond if the economic news appears favorable but price still fails to overcome 52,612.

That would suggest that improving macroeconomic sentiment has not yet translated into sufficient buying strength at the chart's key resistance.

The takeaway for Dow Jones traders and investors

Dow Jones futures have made meaningful technical progress.

The breakout, subsequent pullback and recovery toward 52,500 suggest that buyers are becoming more effective, and the market has so far avoided revisiting the early-October lows.

But the next test matters more than simply celebrating the recent advance.

The 52,612-52,700 region is where the bullish recovery needs to demonstrate that it can overcome previous selling pressure.

The macroeconomic picture adds another layer of uncertainty. Inflation remains elevated, the Fed is avoiding firm guidance, AI financing concerns have not disappeared and lower Treasury yields may reflect more than one economic interpretation.

For traders, the immediate question is whether futures can break resistance and hold recovered ground. For longer-term investors, the broader issue is whether corporate earnings and economic activity remain resilient under relatively restrictive financial conditions.

The same news can produce different market reactions depending on what investors were expecting beforehand.

That is why I would pay particular attention to how futures respond at the identified technical levels rather than assuming that any single headline must produce a predetermined outcome.

Technical levels reflect the October 16, 2026 morning snapshot, not continuously updated quotes. Futures trading involves risk, and the levels discussed are for educational analysis.

This article was written by Itai Levitan at investinglive.com.

item.title: European stock market open: Equities find some footing after a volatile week
item.description:
• Eurostoxx +0.5%
  • Germany DAX +0.7%
  • France CAC 40 -0.2%
  • UK FTSE 100 -0.2%
  • Spain IBEX +0.5%
  • Italy FTSE MIB +0.6%

European equities are finding some relief today, with most major indices posting modest gains as we approach the end of what has been a rather volatile trading week. The French benchmark index is the notable laggard, with fiscal risks continuing to weigh this week.

For now though, I wouldn't read too much into the early advance just yet. Broader markets have had plenty to digest in trading this week, not least with hotter-than-expected US inflation data from both the CPI and PPI reports. That continues to pose fresh questions on the Fed outlook as well as the bond market selloff, even though there is a much calmer tone in the latter in the past few sessions.

While there Treasury yields and the dollar have eased a fair bit, that doesn't necessarily mean investors are out of the woods. The bigger concern remains that inflation pressures are proving to be more stubborn than hoped, leaving central banks with less room to support growth if economic conditions start to deteriorate. And that will be especially difficult for European stocks to navigate through, given the region's own economic and fiscal challenges.

The overall market mood today is at least helped by a steadier showing in US futures. The late recovery in tech shares overnight is carrying over a little, with S&P 500 futures up 0.1% and Nasdaq futures keeping little changed.

Still, I would be cautious about labelling this as a proper turnaround. European stocks are just about managing to find their feet again but whether they can stay on them is another matter entirely.

This article was written by Justin Low at investinglive.com.
